ketubot-2b-11-11.note: A man gives agents a divorce document, saying it takes effect if he does not return within thirty days. He arrives before the deadline, but the ferry is on the far bank and he cannot cross, so he calls out to the people across the river that he has come. Shmuel rules this does not count as a return, so the divorce takes effect. From this the Gemara infers that, apparently, a condition counts as fulfilled even when circumstances beyond his control caused it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: a Babylonian sage who gives the ruling

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives to end a marriage.

ketubot-3a-9-9.note: The Gemara repeats the case of a man who tells agents holding his divorce document that it takes effect if he does not return within thirty days. He reaches the river in time but the ferry on the other side keeps him from crossing. Shmuel rules that this is not a return, so the divorce takes effect. This is brought as further proof that a condition counts as met even when it failed through circumstances beyond his control.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: a Babylonian sage who gives the ruling

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives to end a marriage.

ketubot-7a-1-1.note: Rav Ami permitted a groom to consummate the marriage on Shabbat even though the marriage contract was not yet written. The Sages objected, since living with a wife without a contract is improper. Rav Ami answered that the bride should take property equal to the contract's value from her husband as a deposit, and then the couple may proceed.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: a sage who gave the ruling

terms.meaning: A written contract that obligates the husband to pay his wife a set sum if the marriage ends.

ketubot-8a-9-9.note: Rav Ashi attended a wedding at Rav Kahana's house and recited all seven wedding blessings on the first day. On later days he recited all of them again only if new guests were present. Otherwise he called the gathering an extension of the original celebration and added only a short phrase, 'in Whose dwelling is joy', in the group invitation to Grace after Meals, plus the sixth blessing.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: host of the wedding

terms.meaning: Blessings recited at a Jewish wedding and at celebratory meals during the following week.
The invitation that opens group Grace after Meals.

ketubot-8a-12-12.note: Ravina arranged his son's match with a woman from Rav Haviva's family and recited the wedding blessing at the betrothal, sure the wedding would happen. The family backed out and the wedding was canceled. Separately, Rav Tahlifa came from Israel and recited six long blessings of his own. The Gemara rules that the law does not follow him and one must use the formula the Sages set.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: arranged his son's marriage

people.name: Rav Taḥlifa
people.about: came from the West, i.e. Eretz Yisrael, to Babylonia

terms.meaning: The first stage of marriage, a binding commitment made before the wedding itself.

ketubot-8b-3-10.note: After Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child died, Reish Lakish came the next day with his speaker, Yehuda bar Nahmani, who recited a series of comfort statements: blessings praising God as the One who revives the dead, for the mourners, for the comforters and for all Israel. One verse he quoted seemed to blame the family's sins, but the Gemara explains he meant that the righteous are taken for a generation's sins, which honors Rav Hiyya. Abaye adds that mourners' words should not predict further deaths. The passage concludes that several blessings are said in the days after burial.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: went with his speaker to comfort Rav Ḥiyya bar Abba

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: teacher of Reish Lakish's sons, whose child died

people.name: Abaye
people.about: suggests rewording the mourners' statement

terms.meaning: A speaker who repeats a sage's words aloud so the crowd can hear them.

ketubot-10a-11-11.note: A groom tells Rabban Gamliel that he found no blood on the wedding night, which suggested his bride had not been a virgin, while the bride insists she was a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asks for the cloth, soaks it in water and launders it, and finds several drops of blood. He tells the groom to go take possession of his acquisition, since she was a virgin and there is no cause for concern.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the sage who decides the case

ketubot-10b-1-1.note: A groom came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said he found no blood, and the bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi brought two maidservants, one a virgin and one not, and seated them on the opening of a wine barrel. The wine's scent came through the mouth of the non-virgin but not the virgin. The bride was then seated on the barrel and the scent did not come through, so he told the groom to take his acquisition, for she is a virgin.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the sage who decides the case

ketubot-10b-3-3.note: A groom tells Rabban Gamliel the Elder he found no blood. The bride says she is from the Dorketi family, whose women have neither menstrual blood nor blood from the loss of virginity. Rabban Gamliel checks with her relatives and finds this is true. He tells the groom to take his wife and says he is fortunate, since blood will never raise a problem for him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: the sage who decides the case

ketubot-10b-6-6.note: A groom tells Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi he found no blood, and the bride says she was a virgin. It was a drought year and their faces were dark from hunger. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had them bathed and fed, and afterward the groom found blood, showing hunger had been the cause. He tells the groom to take his wife and quotes a verse about skin withered on the bones.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the sage who decides the case

ketubot-12b-0-0.note: The court saw priests treating widows with disrespect, so it set a marriage contract of two hundred dinars for widows to raise their standing. Then men began avoiding widows from priestly families, preferring to marry virgin Israelite women for the same price. So the court restored the earlier arrangement. The Gemara concludes that the mishna and the baraita speak of different periods and different rules.

terms.meaning: A marriage contract that sets the sum a husband owes his wife if the marriage ends.
A teaching from the early rabbis that was not included in the Mishna.

ketubot-14b-11-11.note: Rabbi Yosei recalls a case of a young girl who went to a spring to fill her jug and was assaulted by an unknown man. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri rules that if most of the city's people marry their daughters to priests, she may marry a priest. The passage gives only that ruling; the story is told to illustrate the legal question.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: reports the incident

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri
people.about: gives the ruling

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, who has special duties and stricter marriage rules.

ketubot-17a-3-3.note: When Rabbi Abbahu came from the study hall to the emperor's house, the emperor's maidservants went out to greet him with a song. They called him master of his people, leader of his nation and a lamp of light, and welcomed his arrival in peace. The Gemara gives this as an example of people praising the Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: a sage who was honored at the emperor's house

ketubot-17a-4-4.note: On the duty to bring joy to a bride and groom, Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai danced before the bride with a myrtle branch, calling her fair and attractive. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggled three myrtle branches while dancing, and Rabbi Zeira complained that this demeaned Torah scholars. The passage ends by saying that when Rav Shmuel died a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign given to only one or two people in a generation.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: danced before brides with a myrtle branch

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak
people.about: juggled three myrtle branches while dancing

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: objected to the juggling

terms.meaning: A fragrant branch traditionally used at weddings.

ketubot-17a-6-6.note: Rav Aha would put the bride on his shoulders and dance. The Sages asked him whether they were also allowed to do this. He answered that if brides seem to them like a beam of wood, they may, but if not, they may not.

people.name: Rav Aḥa
people.about: danced with the bride on his shoulders

ketubot-17a-8-8.note: A teaching says a funeral procession must give way to a bride's wedding procession, and both give way to a king of Israel. It then tells how King Agrippa, though he did not have to, rerouted his own entourage to make way for a bride's procession. The Sages praised him for it.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: a king who gave way to a bride's wedding procession

ketubot-20a-2-3.note: Bar Shatya suffered bouts of insanity. After he sold his property, one pair of witnesses said he sold it while insane and another pair said he was sane. Rav Nahman and Rav Ashi say the two pairs cancel each other, so the property stays with its current holder. The Gemara adds that this keeps it with Bar Shatya only if he inherited it from his fathers. If he bought it himself, he may have bought it while insane, so it stays with the buyer.

people.name: Bar Shatya
people.about: a man who suffered periodic bouts of insanity

terms.meaning: The legal assumption that whoever holds property is its rightful owner unless proven otherwise.

ketubot-22a-9-9.note: A strikingly beautiful woman told her many suitors she was already engaged. Later she got engaged to a man, and the Sages asked why. She said she had said it to put off unscrupulous men, and now respectable ones had come. When the question was raised in Usha, the Sages ruled that if she gives a reason for her statement, she is believed.

people.name: Rav Aḥa Sar HaBira
people.about: raised the question before the Sages in Usha

terms.meaning: The first stage of marriage, binding the couple before the wedding itself.

ketubot-23a-13-16.note: Captive women were brought to Neharde'a to be ransomed, and Shmuel's father posted guards so they would not be alone with gentiles. Shmuel asked who had guarded them until now, and his father answered: would you treat them with such contempt if they were your daughters? The father's words were "like an error that emerges from before the ruler" and came true: Shmuel's own daughters were taken captive and brought to Eretz Yisrael. Leaving their captors outside, they went into Rabbi Hanina's study hall, each said "I was taken captive and I am pure", and the court permitted them to marry priests. When the captors then came in, the permission stood because the daughters had spoken first. Once it became clear they were Shmuel's daughters, Rabbi Hanina told Rav Shemen bar Abba, a priest, to marry one of them. Rav Shemen objected that there were witnesses overseas. Rabbi Hanina answered that those witnesses are not here. The Gemara infers that if the witnesses did come, the daughters would be forbidden to priests.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: a Babylonian sage, whose daughters were captured

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: the sage in Eretz Yisrael whose court permitted the daughters

people.name: Rav Shemen bar Abba
people.about: a priest whom Rabbi Ḥanina told to marry one of them

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, who has stricter marriage rules, including limits on marrying a woman who may have been defiled in captivity.

ketubot-26a-0-1.note: A man spoke casually about remembering, as a small child, being taken out of school and immersed so he could eat teruma, the food reserved for priests. His friends then kept their distance and called him 'Yohanan who eats ḥallot'. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted his offhand statement and treated him as a priest. The point is that a person's casual remark is reliable, and so is one about his brother.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: accepted the man's statement and elevated him to priesthood

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: related the incident

terms.meaning: A portion of produce set aside for priests, which only priests may eat.
A portion of dough given to priests, eaten only by them.

ketubot-26b-7-7.note: Rava quotes a mishna about a Jewish woman who witnesses say was held as collateral for a debt in Ashkelon. Her family suspected she had been violated and kept away from her, but other witnesses said she had neither been alone with a man nor assaulted. The Sages told the family to trust the witnesses on both points or neither, and in either case she is permitted to her husband.

people.name: Rava
people.about: raises the mishna as an objection

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: testified about the case

people.name: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav
people.about: testified about the case

terms.meaning: A man and woman being alone together in private, which the law treats as a possibility for forbidden relations.

ketubot-27b-1-2.note: A man rented a donkey on condition that it not be taken along the Pekod River path, where it might drown, and the donkey died. The renter told Rava he used that path but there was no water, so something else killed it. Rava accepted his claim because he could have lied and said he took the other path. Abaye objected that the 'why would I lie' argument fails when it contradicts known facts, since everyone knows the river has water there. The passage concludes that his claim is not accepted.

people.name: Rava
people.about: the judge who accepts the claim

people.name: Abaye
people.about: objects to Rava

terms.meaning: A principle that a person is believed if he could have told a more convincing lie but chose to tell a less helpful version.

ketubot-27b-10-11.note: A man from a distant district told Mari bar Isak he was his brother and asked for a share of their father's property, but Mari said he did not know him. Rav Hisda said Mari was right to not recognize him and cited Joseph, whose brothers did not recognize him once he had a beard. Rav Hisda asked the claimant for witnesses, but he said they were afraid of Mari. Rav Hisda then ordered Mari, a known violent man, to bring witnesses that this was not his brother. The Gemara concludes that a person is not suspected of both hiding the truth and lying.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: the man who denied knowing the claimant

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: the judge who decided the case

terms.meaning: The responsibility of the person making a claim to bring evidence, which Rav Hisda reverses here for violent men.

ketubot-28a-5-6.note: A man who had divorced his betrothed brought a case before Rava, and Rava had an intermediary placed between the two. Rav Adda bar Mattana objected, citing Rav Nahman's teaching that a woman divorced from betrothal is paid directly. Rava replied that this applies only to people who are not familiar with each other, and here the two are, so they must be kept apart. A second version has the roles reversed, with Rav Adda urging the intermediary and Rava citing the objection, but the same conclusion follows.

people.name: Rava
people.about: the judge

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: sat before Rava and raised the objection

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: his teaching is cited

terms.meaning: A woman in the first stage of marriage, committed to a man but not yet fully married.

ketubot-28b-3-4.note: A teaching quotes Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei, saying he testified only once, and the court raised a slave to priesthood on his word. The Gemara says this cannot be right, because God would not cause such a mistake through a righteous person. It corrects the statement: they wanted to do so, but in the end did not. He had seen a priest's slave given teruma in Rabbi Yosei's town, where this is not proof of priesthood, and he then testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's town, where it is.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: the witness who testified

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their household may eat.

ketubot-49b-6-6.note: The Gemara says a man is made to support his children only when he can afford it, while a wealthy man can be forced. It brings the case of Rava, who forced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give to charity and collected four hundred dinars from him. This shows the court can compel a person to give charity if he can afford it. By the same reasoning, it applies even more to supporting his own children.

people.name: Rava
people.about: collected charity by force

people.name: Rav Natan bar Ami
people.about: a wealthy man forced to give charity

terms.meaning: Charity, meaning giving to those in need.

ketubot-49b-12-12.note: Scholars ask whether the law follows Rabbi Ile'a's view about a father being supported by his children. As evidence, the Gemara tells of a man who kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot, because the man had given his property to his sons and Rabbi Yonatan forced them to feed him. The Gemara reasons that if the sons were legally required to support him, the court could simply have taken the money from the property, so forcing them suggests they were not required. It concludes the law does not follow Rabbi Ile'a.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the accepted ruling.

ketubot-50a-10-10.note: Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina said the Sages at Usha ruled that if a wife sells property whose produce belongs to her husband and then dies, the husband can take it back from the buyers. Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef found Rabbi Abbahu in Usha and asked who had spread this ruling. Rabbi Abbahu named Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina. Rav Yitzhak then learned it from him forty times, until he remembered it as if it were in his pocket.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina
people.about: reported the Usha ordinance

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: learned the ruling forty times

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: the sage he asked and learned from

terms.meaning: A wife's property whose produce belongs to her husband while the property itself stays hers.

ketubot-52b-4-5.note: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for daily treatment of their father's widow, who was owed support. Rabbi Yohanan told them to agree a lump sum with the doctor, so the cost would be fixed and deducted from her marriage contract. He later regretted this, saying they had acted like legal advisors helping people find loopholes. The Gemara says he first followed the verse about not hiding from one's own flesh, but later held that an important person helping family at another's expense looks like favoritism.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: the sage who advised his relatives

terms.meaning: A written contract that sets the sum a husband owes his wife if the marriage ends.

ketubot-54a-13-14.note: A woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. He heard from her accent that she was from Mehoza and began to apply Rav's ruling, which applies in Babylonia. When told she was marrying a man from Neharde'a, he said the ruling of Shmuel, followed in Neharde'a, applies. The Gemara adds that the area of Neharde'a extends as far as places using its measurement system.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: the judge in the case

people.name: Rav
people.about: his opinion is followed in Babylonia

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: his opinion is followed in Neharde'a

terms.meaning: A written contract that sets the sum a husband owes his wife if the marriage ends.

ketubot-54a-22-22.note: Two short cases follow. A man's will told his heirs to give his daughter four hundred dinars' worth of his wine; the wine rose in value, leaving extra money, and Rav Yosef ruled the extra goes to the sons. Then the sons of Rabbi Yohanan's relatives complained that their father's wife was wastefully draining his estate; Rabbi Yohanan advised having the father set aside land for her support, which, if she accepts it, ends her claim on the rest of the estate.

terms.meaning: Here, the heirs of a man who has died.

ketubot-54b-1-2.note: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives were struggling because their father's wife was spending wastefully on her upkeep. Rabbi Yohanan advised setting aside a piece of land for her support, which she would then accept in place of her claim on the rest. After the father died, Reish Lakish ruled that they must still support her fully and she could also use the field. They objected that Rabbi Yohanan had said otherwise and Reish Lakish threatened them. Rabbi Yohanan told them he could not override a colleague of equal standing who disagrees.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: gave the earlier advice

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: ruled after the father died

ketubot-60a-2-2.note: A divorced woman did not want to nurse her son and came before Shmuel. Shmuel sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to check whether the child knew her. Rav Dimi placed her in a row of women and carried the child past them. The baby looked at her face with joy while she looked away, so he told her to look up and take her son, because the baby clearly knew her. The Gemara then asks how a blind baby recognizes his mother, and Rav Ashi answers: by smell and the taste of her milk.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: the sage before whom the woman came

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: carried out the test

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: answers the question about a blind baby

ketubot-60b-2-3.note: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after the birth. Abaye allowed it, citing rulings that follow Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel, plus Ulla's and Mar Ukva's statements. Rav Yosef then told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require a wait of twenty-four months even before betrothal. Abaye ran after the farmer to warn him, but could not catch him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the sage who gave the ruling and then ran after the farmer

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: corrected Abaye

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: require waiting twenty-four months

terms.meaning: The first stage of marriage, a binding commitment made before the wedding itself.
An ancient Persian measure of distance, a few miles.

ketubot-60b-5-9.note: A teaching says a nursing mother may remarry right away if she gave the baby to a wet nurse, weaned him, or he died. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna meant to act on it, but an old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden it. Rav Pappi pointed out that Rabbi Meir, whose rulings Rav Nahman says to follow, requires a three-month wait. The Gemara concludes that the wait is waived only if the child died; some add that even then it applies, though a case of a mother strangling her baby is dismissed as insanity.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
Rav Naḥman
people.about: his ruling is cited by the old woman

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: his strict view is followed

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbis that was not included in the Mishna.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

ketubot-61a-14-14.note: The Gemara tells of two pious men, said by some to be Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, sons of Rav Hisda. One fed his waiter before the meal and the other fed him after the guests had eaten. Elijah the prophet spoke with the one who fed the waiter first, but not with the other. The text does not state the reason, but it follows a discussion about meal etiquette.

people.name: Rav Mari and Rav Pineḥas
people.about: sons of Rav Ḥisda, according to some

people.name: Elijah
people.about: the prophet, who spoke to one of them

ketubot-61a-15-15.note: Rav Ashi, Ameimar and Mar Zutra sat at King Izgur's gate while the king's food was carried past. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra go pale from craving and put a bit of the food into his mouth. The royal staff said he had spoiled the king's meal, but he said the cook had, because he saw a leprous mark in the meat. They found nothing until he pointed to the exact spot, where it then appeared. Asked how he knew, he said he saw a leprous spirit hovering over the food.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: fed Mar Zutra a bit of the food

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: craved the king's food

ketubot-61b-1-1.note: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He peeled pomegranates and ate them in front of her without sharing, and the smell made her mouth water until she swallowed her saliva and grew ill and bloated. He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed. He ate pomegranates again and told her to spit out the saliva. She did, until something like a green leaf came out, and she was cured. The text does not say whether she married him.

ketubot-62a-4-4.note: A Jew and a gentile were walking together, and the gentile could not keep up with the faster Jew. He reminded him of the destruction of the Temple so that he would sigh and slow down. The Jew groaned but still walked faster, and the gentile asked why the groaning had not weakened him. The Jew replied that this only applies to a new grief; people grow used to old tragedies, like a mother used to losing children.

ketubot-62a-7-7.note: To show the strength of people in Eretz Yisrael, the Gemara tells two stories. When a bathhouse collapsed under Rabbi Abbahu, he climbed onto a pillar and pulled up the two slaves supporting him. Rabbi Yohanan did the same when a staircase collapsed under him and his two supporters. Asked why he needs support if he is so strong, Rabbi Yohanan said he was saving his strength for old age.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: survived the bathhouse collapse

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: survived the staircase collapse

people.name: Rav Ami and Rav Asi
people.about: were supporting Rabbi Yoḥanan

ketubot-62b-3-3.note: Rav Rehumi studied under Rava and usually came home each year on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he was absorbed in his learning and stayed behind, while his wife kept waiting for him and finally wept. At that moment the roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died. The Gemara learns from this how careful a person must be not to cause his wife anguish, even by accident.

people.name: Rav Reḥumi
people.about: a student of Rava in Meḥoza

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.

ketubot-62b-5-5.note: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, usually came home every Shabbat eve, preceded by a pillar of fire that Rabbi Yannai saw. One day he stayed behind absorbed in study, and without the sign Rabbi Yannai told the family to turn his bed over as in mourning, assuming he had died. The text says that his words came true like a ruler's mistake, and Yehuda died.

people.name: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: a student who stayed in the study hall

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: his father-in-law, who assumed he had died

terms.meaning: A mourning custom in which beds are turned over.

ketubot-62b-6-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tried to marry his son into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died; a check of family descent found a possible reason. He then arranged a match with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's household, where the son was to study for twelve years. On seeing the bride the son married first and then went to study, and his father said this was like God's own conduct. After twelve years of study the son returned to find his wife unable to have children, and he prayed and she was cured.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: arranged his son's marriage

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: the family of the first bride

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
people.about: the family of the second bride

ketubot-62b-10-11.note: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left a wedding feast to study Torah, though Rabbi Shimon asked him to wait for him. He stayed in the study hall twelve years, and when he returned the roads had changed and he could not find his house. He heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and followed her home. His wife saw him and died from the shock, but he prayed to God and she came back to life.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Ḥakhinai
people.about: the scholar who studied for twelve years

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: asked him to wait

ketubot-62b-12-13.note: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied twelve years away, and on his return, determined not to shock his wife as Ben Hakhinai had, he sat in the town's study hall and sent word he had arrived. A young man he did not recognize asked sharp legal questions, and Rabbi Hama sadly wished he had taught his own son like that. At home he stood up to honor the young man, and his wife asked if a father stands for his son. The young man was his son Rabbi Oshaya, described as the third generation of scholars in the family.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa
people.about: returned after twelve years of study

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: his son, whom he did not recognize

ketubot-62b-14-14.note: Ben Kalba Savua, a wealthy man of Jerusalem, had a shepherd named Akiva. His daughter saw that Akiva was humble and refined, and she betrothed herself to him in secret on condition that he go to study Torah. Her angry father threw her out and vowed that she could not benefit from his property. After twelve years Akiva came back with twelve thousand students. He overheard his wife say she would gladly have him study another twelve years, so he went back. He returned with twenty-four thousand students. When his attendants pushed her away, he told them that his learning and theirs was hers. Her father, hoping to have his vow annulled, learned that Akiva was the man, kissed his feet and gave him half his money. Rabbi Akiva's daughter later did the same for ben Azzai, which explains the saying: the ewe follows the ewe.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: the shepherd who became a great sage

people.name: Akiva's wife
people.about: daughter of ben Kalba Savua, who sent him to study

people.name: Ben Kalba Savua
people.about: her wealthy father in Jerusalem

people.name: Ben Azzai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's daughter betrothed herself to him and sent him to study

terms.meaning: A solemn promise that can be annulled only by a sage if the person regrets it.

ketubot-63a-2-2.note: Rav Yosef, son of Rava, was sent by his father to study with the great Rav Yosef, and they agreed on six years. After three years, on the eve of Yom Kippur, he said he would go see his wife. His father took a weapon, went to meet him, and rebuked him in sharp words for abandoning his studies for a woman. In their quarrel neither ate the meal before the Yom Kippur fast. The text does not say whether he went home.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: the student who wanted to see his wife

people.name: Rava
people.about: his father, who confronted him

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: the great Sage he was sent to study with

terms.meaning: The meal eaten before the fast of Yom Kippur begins.

ketubot-63b-8-8.note: When Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband, three Sages said she loses her right to her worn clothes. Rav Gamda objected that they were flattering Rav Zevid, since Rava had left this question unresolved. In another version they ruled the opposite, and he gave the same objection. The conclusion is that since the question is undecided, if she already holds the item it is not taken from her, but if she does not, it is not given to her.

terms.meaning: Here, a wife who refuses to live with her husband as a wife.

ketubot-65a-8-9.note: After Abaye died, his widow Homa asked Rava, the local judge, for support and then for wine. Rava refused the wine because Abaye did not drink it, but she showed how large his cups were, and her bared arm shone with beauty. Rava went home and asked his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, for intimacy. When she learned that Homa had been in court, she chased Homa out of Mehoza with the lock of a chest. She said Homa had already killed three husbands and was now coming to kill Rava, who would want to marry her.

people.name: Ḥoma
people.about: Abaye's widow, who came before Rava

people.name: Rava
people.about: the judge

people.name: Rava's wife
people.about: daughter of Rav Ḥisda

ketubot-66b-10-13.note: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman picking barley out of animal dung, covering herself with her hair. She was the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon, once so wealthy that her marriage contract listed a million gold dinars from her father's house. He wept and said that when Israel does God's will no nation rules them, and when it does not, they are handed to a lowly nation. The Gemara asks whether Nakdimon did not give charity, and offers two possible answers: he gave for his own honor, or he gave less than he should have. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swears that he saw her gathering barley among horses' hooves in Akko.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: met the woman and wept

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: her once-wealthy father

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: said he saw her gathering barley in Akko

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbis that was not included in the Mishna.

ketubot-67b-2-2.note: The Sages read a verse about helping a poor person as meaning you must cover what he lacks, but you need not make him rich. For someone used to a comfortable life, that lack can include a horse to ride and a servant to run in front of him. Hillel the Elder once got a poor man of good family exactly that. When no servant could be found one day, Hillel ran in front of him himself for three mil.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: a famous Sage

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
The part of the Talmud that discusses and explains the earlier teachings.

ketubot-67b-4-4.note: A man asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity and said he normally ate fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share a simple meal of lentils, and the man died because his body was not used to that food. Rabbi Nehemya said, 'Woe to this one who was killed by Nehemya.' The Gemara first suggests he should have blamed himself, then explains he meant the man was at fault for pampering himself so much.

terms.meaning: The part of the Talmud that discusses and explains the earlier teachings.

ketubot-67b-5-6.note: A man asked Rava for charity and said he usually ate fattened hen and aged wine. When Rava asked if he worried about burdening the community, the man answered that he was eating from God's support, not theirs. Just then Rava's sister, who had not seen him in thirteen years, arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine as a gift. Rava took this as a sign that the man was right and told him to get up and eat.

people.name: Rava
people.about: a Sage of the Talmud

people.name: Rava's sister
people.about: had not seen him for thirteen years

terms.meaning: A name for God used in the Talmud.

ketubot-67b-11-12.note: Mar Ukva secretly tossed four dinars to a poor neighbor every day. One day the neighbor tried to see who it was, and Mar Ukva and his wife ran off and hid in a furnace whose fire was low but still burning. His feet were burned, and his wife told him to rest them on hers, which were not burned. When he was upset, she explained that she gives food directly at home, so her help is more immediate than his money.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: gave charity in secret

terms.meaning: A silver coin used as money.

ketubot-67b-14-14.note: Every year before Yom Kippur, Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor man. His son brought the money and came back saying the man did not need it, since he had seen old wine being poured on the ground to make the room smell nice. Mar Ukva replied that someone this used to luxury needs even more money, and he doubled the gift.

people.name: Mar Ukva's son
people.about: carried the money to the poor man

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.

ketubot-67b-15-15.note: As Mar Ukva was dying, he checked his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He felt this was too little to take with him to the World-to-Come, so he gave away half of his remaining money. The Gemara asks how he could do this, since a rule from Usha limits giving to one-fifth. It answers that the limit applies only during life, to avoid becoming poor, and not after death.

people.name: Rabbi Ilai
people.about: quoted for the Usha rule

terms.meaning: The afterlife, where a person's good deeds are rewarded.
A place where the Sages gathered and made rulings.

ketubot-69a-14-16.note: Rav Anan wrote to Rav Huna, addressing him as "Huna, our friend", and asked him to give a woman one-tenth of her father's estate. Rav Huna sent a sharp reply through Rav Sheshet, under threat of excommunication if the reply was not passed on word for word. The reply said: "Anan, Anan", should the tenth come from real estate or from movable property, and who sits at the head in the house of a marzeiha? Rav Anan, offended and not knowing the word, went to Mar Ukva. Mar Ukva said that a man who does not know what a marzeiha is has no business calling Rav Huna "our friend". The Gemara explains that a marzeiha is a mourner.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: carried Rav Huna's reply

terms.meaning: A mourner, a person in a house of mourning.
Being formally cut off from the community as a penalty.

ketubot-69b-10-12.note: Rabbi Yohanan was chosen as head of the yeshiva instead of Ilfa, who was away. Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and said he would drown if anyone could cite a teaching he could not trace to a mishna. An older man cited a ruling on a dying father who says to give his sons a shekel a week, and Ilfa answered that it follows Rabbi Meir, who says to carry out the wishes of the dead. The passage then continues with Mar Ukva's ruling and a new mishna, which are discussion rather than story.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: a Sage passed over as head of the yeshiva

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: chosen as head of the yeshiva

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: his view is used in Ilfa's answer

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishna that was not included in the Mishna.
A school for studying Torah.

ketubot-72b-3-3.note: Rabba bar bar Hanna told of walking behind Rav Ukva and seeing an Arab woman sitting and spinning a red thread opposite her face. When she saw them, she tore the spindle from the thread, threw it down and said to him, "Young man, give me the spindle." Rav Ukva remarked that she was an example of one of the kinds of improper behavior listed in the mishna. The passage ends with a disagreement about which kind: Ravina says spinning in the marketplace, and the Rabbis say speaking with every man.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hanna
people.about: tells the story

people.name: Ravina
people.about: gives one view of what Rav Ukva meant

terms.meaning: The early collection of Jewish law that the Talmud discusses.

ketubot-77b-5-8.note: The passage opens with how Sages treated people with the disease ra'atan: some kept away, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi studied Torah with them. When he was dying, he asked the Angel of Death to show him his place in paradise and to lend him his knife, then jumped into paradise and swore he would not come back. God ruled that he could stay because he had never asked to have an oath dissolved, and a Divine Voice told him to give the knife back. Elijah announced his arrival. Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai asked him whether a rainbow had appeared in his lifetime. He said yes, so Rabbi Shimon doubted he was truly righteous, but the Gemara says no rainbow had ever appeared and he answered yes only out of modesty.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: a righteous Sage

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: found sitting in paradise

people.name: Elijah the Prophet
people.about: announced his arrival

terms.meaning: A contagious disease the Sages feared catching.
Asking a judge to cancel a vow one has made.

ketubot-77b-9-11.note: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, a friend of the Angel of Death, asked for thirty days to review his learning before dying. Later he tried the same knife trick as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but the angel noted he had not studied with people with ra'atan as Rabbi Yehoshua had. When he died, a pillar of fire kept everyone away until Rabbi Alexandri asked it to leave in the dead Sage's own honor. The passage closes with Abaye and Rav Adda bar Mattana debating what the fire meant.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa
people.about: friend of the Angel of Death

people.name: Rabbi Alexandri
people.about: persuaded the fire to disappear

people.name: Abaye
people.about: offers an explanation of the fire

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: answers Abaye

terms.meaning: A contagious disease the Sages feared catching.

ketubot-78b-11-11.note: A woman about to remarry gave her property to her daughter on paper, only to keep it from her future husband. After she divorced, she asked for it back and the daughter said it was a gift. Rav Nahman tore up the document, accepting that it was never meant as a real transfer. Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva, who cited Shmuel's ruling that such a document of evasion should be torn up. When Rava asked his reason, Rav Nahman said the mother put her own interests before her daughter's.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: the judge who tore the document

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: complained about the ruling

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: called the Exilarch in the text

people.name: Rava
people.about: asked Rav Nahman for his reason

terms.meaning: A deed written to hide property from someone, with no real intent to transfer it.
The leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

ketubot-80a-4-5.note: A woman was left 400 dinars in a faraway place. Her husband spent 600 of his own dinars to go and bring it back, and used one dinar of her money on the way. Rabbi Ami ruled that what he spent and what he ate are settled, so neither side can claim it from the other. When the Rabbis objected that he had eaten from the principal, Rabbi Ami said that for his expenses he could swear how much he paid and then take that amount.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: the judge who ruled

terms.meaning: A silver coin used as money.
The original property itself, as opposed to the profit or produce it brings in.

ketubot-80b-1-2.note: A woman brought two maidservants into the marriage as part of her dowry. Her husband then married a second wife and gave one of the maidservants to her. The first wife complained to Rava, but he paid no attention. The text says one might think Rava allowed it because a husband may do as he likes with his wife's property, but the real reason is that the Sages gave a husband the produce of her property for the household's benefit, and the maidservant still works for the house.

people.name: Rava
people.about: the judge

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: explains the incident

terms.meaning: The right to use something and enjoy its produce without owning it.

ketubot-82b-9-12.note: Rav Yehuda describes how the marriage contract developed. At first a large sum had to be set aside in cash, so many men could not afford to marry. The Sages then moved the money to the bride's father's house, then to the husband's house, but a husband in a rage could still say 'take your contract and go.' Finally Shimon ben Shatah ruled that all the husband's property guarantees the sum, which made divorce costlier and so harder to do on a whim.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: tells the history

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: made the final ordinance

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband promises his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.
A teaching from the time of the Mishna that was not included in the Mishna.

ketubot-84b-7-7.note: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives took a cow belonging to orphans because the orphans' father had owed them money. Rabbi Yohanan said they could keep it, following Rabbi Tarfon. Reish Lakish told them to give it back. When they complained, Rabbi Yohanan said he could not dismiss the opinion of someone as great as himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: allowed the seizure

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: ordered the cow returned

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: his view was relied on by Rabbi Yohanan

terms.meaning: Here, the children of a man who died owing money.

ketubot-84b-10-10.note: Members of the household of the prince of Eretz Yisrael took a maidservant belonging to orphans to cover a debt their father owed. Rabbi Abbahu, one of the judges, said it was fine that they took her. Rabbi Abba objected that the judges were flattering the prince's household. He pointed out that Reish Lakish had overturned a similar seizure, showing the law does not follow Rabbi Tarfon.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: approved the seizure

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: objected

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: mentioned for overturning a similar seizure

terms.meaning: The leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.

ketubot-84b-11-11.note: A man named Yeimar bar Hashu was owed money by a dead man who left a boat, and he sent an agent to seize it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, who were also owed money, said such a seizure harms the other creditors, and then each took the boat for himself. Rava called them unlawful grabbers, since the boat was taken after the debtor's death, when his heirs already held it. The rule that whoever seizes first acquires it applies only when seized from the debtor while he was alive.

people.name: Yeimar bar Hashu
people.about: the creditor who sent an agent

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
Rava
people.about: gave the ruling

terms.meaning: A person who is owed money.
Jewish law.

ketubot-85a-3-4.note: Avimi owed money to people from Bei Hozai and sent it with Hama, who paid it and asked for the debt document back. They refused, saying the payment covered a different, unwritten debt, so the written one was still unpaid. Rabbi Abbahu asked Hama if he had witnesses to the payment, and Hama had none. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since they could have denied being paid at all, their claim of a side debt is believed, so Hama gets neither the money nor the document.

people.name: Avimi, son of Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: the man who owed the money

people.name: Hama, son of Rabba bar Abbahu
people.about: paid on Avimi's behalf

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: gave the ruling

terms.meaning: A legal principle: if a person could have made a stronger claim and did not, we believe the weaker claim he made.

ketubot-85a-8-10.note: A woman had to swear an oath in Rava's court, but Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, said she knew the woman lied under oath. Rava passed the oath to the other side, who could swear and collect. In a second case, Rav Pappa said he knew a document's debt had been paid, but Rava would not rely on one witness. Rava explained he trusted his wife because he knew she was always truthful, but did not know that of Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rava
people.about: the judge

people.name: Daughter of Rav Hisda
people.about: Rava's wife

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: the single witness about the document

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: asked why Rav Pappa was not trusted

terms.meaning: A sworn statement in court that can settle who wins a money dispute.

ketubot-85a-13-14.note: A woman had to take an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court. The other side asked that she swear in the town, hoping shame would make her admit the truth. She asked for a document guaranteeing her rights first, and Rav Beivai told them to write it for her. Rav Pappi then rebuked him, saying that people from an unfortunate family say unfortunate things, a reference to the house of Eli.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: the judge, from the house of Eli according to the text

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: rebuked him

terms.meaning: A written statement protecting a person's claim.

ketubot-85b-9-9.note: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her marriage contract, was later divorced, and died, leaving the right to her daughter. The buyers then claimed the money from the daughter. Rav Nahman said someone should advise the daughter to forgive her father's debt, so the buyers get nothing and she inherits from him later. She did so, and Rav Nahman then regretted acting like a lawyer for a litigant instead of a judge, though the Gemara says he first thought helping family was right.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: the judge who gave the advice

people.name: Rav Nahman's relative
people.about: sold her marriage contract

people.name: Her daughter
people.about: followed the advice

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband promises his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

ketubot-86a-4-4.note: This passage briefly says there was a similar case in which Rafram pressured Rav Ashi to give a clear ruling. Rav Ashi then collected the full value of the debt listed in the promissory note. It does not say what the case was, so the situation and the reason are missing.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: pressured Rav Ashi

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: collected the full value

terms.meaning: A written promise to pay a debt.

ketubot-91a-19-20.note: A man named bar Tzartzur left little property beyond what his wives' marriage contracts were worth, and it later rose in value. His sons from the two wives disputed it before Rav Amram, who told the sons of the wife with the bigger contract to give some to the others. They refused, so he threatened excommunication and sent them to Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman ruled that the heirs divide the whole estate equally, based on its value when the father died.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: first judge, threatened excommunication

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: gave the final ruling

people.name: Bar Tzartzur
people.about: the man who died

terms.meaning: Being formally cut off from the community as a penalty.
A document in which a husband promises his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

ketubot-91b-2-3.note: A man owed a creditor one thousand dinars and sold two mansions for five hundred each. The creditor took one mansion from a buyer, then came for the second. The buyer offered the creditor the full thousand dinars to give up both. Rami bar Hama compared this to a rule that orphans cannot inflate a property's value, but Rava said the cases differ: here the creditor loses nothing, so it would be cruel for him to refuse the money.

terms.meaning: Someone who is owed money.
Here, the heirs of a man who has died.

ketubot-91b-8-9.note: A man owed a creditor one hundred dinars and sold two small fields for fifty each. The creditor took one field from a buyer, then came for the other. The buyer offered the full hundred dinars so the creditor would give up both fields. Rav Yosef compared this to a rule that orphans cannot inflate a property's value, but Abaye said the creditor loses nothing here, so it would be cruel of him to refuse the money.

terms.meaning: Someone who is owed money.
Here, the heirs of a man who has died.

ketubot-91b-12-13.note: A man died owing a creditor 100 dinars and left only a small field worth 50. The creditor took the field, and the orphans paid him 50 dinars to get it back, but he took it again to collect the rest of the debt. The orphans complained to Abaye, who ruled against them. Their payment fulfilled the mitzva of paying their father's debt, but it did not cancel the creditor's claim on the field, so he took it lawfully.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: a rabbi of the Talmud who ruled on the case

terms.meaning: a commandment or good deed required by Jewish law.
a creditor's legal claim on property to secure a debt.

ketubot-91b-15-15.note: A man sold his right to collect his mother's marriage contract payment (if he later inherited it), saying he would not repay the buyer if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he himself then contested the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he could object in her place. Rava replied that although he did not guarantee against her objection, he did guarantee against his own, so the sale stands.

terms.meaning: The ketubah, a written sum a husband owes his wife on divorce or death.

ketubot-94b-6-9.note: Rami bar Hama's mother wrote a deed giving her property to him in the morning, and another giving it to his brother Mar Ukva in the evening. Rav Sheshet awarded the property to Rami, and Rav Nahman awarded it to Mar Ukva. Rav Sheshet's reason was that Rami's deed came first. Rav Nahman answered that deeds in their place do not record the hour, so the order in a day does not matter. Rav Nahman said he ruled by the judges' discretion, judging what the mother wanted. He added that he is a judge and Rav Sheshet is not, so his ruling stands.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: son who got the morning deed

people.name: Mar Ukva bar Hama
people.about: his brother, who got the evening deed

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: ruled for Rami

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: ruled for Mar Ukva

terms.meaning: the judges' power to decide by what seems to be the person's real intention when the law gives no clear answer.

ketubot-94b-10-12.note: Two buyers brought deeds for the same field to Rav Yosef. One deed was dated the fifth of Nisan and the other said only Nisan. Rav Yosef awarded the field to the one with the exact date, since the other could have been written on the 29th. The loser asked for a document letting him take the seller's other property. Rav Yosef said someone could answer that his deed may actually be the earlier one, so he should take that field instead. The Gemara's solution is that the two deed holders write documents authorizing each other to collect.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: the rabbi who judged the case

terms.meaning: a month in the Jewish calendar, in spring.
a court document allowing someone to collect a debt from property the debtor sold to others.

ketubot-98a-6-7.note: Someone was holding coral that belonged to orphans. He valued it for himself at 400 dinars and took it. The coral then rose in value to 600 dinars, and he asked Rabbi Ammi who gets the profit. Rabbi Ammi asked who had valued it for him. Since no court or orphans had sold it to him, he never acquired it, so it stayed the orphans' and the profit is theirs.

people.name: Rabbi Ammi
people.about: the rabbi who ruled on the case

ketubot-100b-17-18.note: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and also had his own wine to take to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the nephew's wine along or should wait for a better time. Rav Ashi told him to take both: the orphan's wine is no worse off than his own, and if he is willing to sell his own that way, he may sell the orphan's the same way.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: the man holding the orphan's wine

people.name: Ravina the younger
people.about: the orphan, his sister's son

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: the rabbi he asked

terms.meaning: the accepted Jewish law on a question.

ketubot-103a-2-3.note: A man rented out his millstone and the renter paid by grinding grain for him. The owner became rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and no longer needed the grinding. He demanded money for the rental instead. The renter replied that he had agreed to grind, not to pay money. The passage ends with the dispute and no ruling.

terms.meaning: a heavy stone used to grind grain into flour.

ketubot-103a-24-32.note: This long passage covers the last days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, editor of the Mishnah. On his deathbed he told his sons to honor their stepmother, kept his lamp, table and bed set as usual, and named Gamliel as Nasi, Shimon as a Sage and Hanina bar Hama to head the yeshiva. The Gemara explains these wishes and adds side stories, such as his Shabbat-eve visits home that stopped when a maidservant gave him away. It ends with him teaching his two sons.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: leader of the Jewish people in his time

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: his older son, named Nasi

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: his younger son, a Sage

people.name: Hanina bar Hama
people.about: named to head the yeshiva

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: a scholar known for teaching Torah to children

terms.meaning: the president or head of the Jewish community and its court.
an academy for Torah study.
the afterlife, where the righteous are rewarded.
a heavenly voice the Talmud describes as announcing a message.

ketubot-103b-3-3.note: On the day Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was buried, a heavenly voice announced that everyone at his funeral was destined for the World-to-Come. A launderer who visited him daily had not come that day and missed the funeral. When he heard Rabbi had died, he was so grief-stricken that he climbed to the roof, fell, and died. The heavenly voice then announced that this launderer, too, was destined for the World-to-Come.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the leader whose funeral it was

terms.meaning: the afterlife, where the righteous are rewarded.
a heavenly voice the Talmud describes as announcing a message.

ketubot-103b-8-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had said that Hanina bar Hama should head the yeshiva. Hanina refused, because Rabbi Afes was older by two and a half years and he would not go ahead of him. So Afes headed the yeshiva, Hanina sat outside, and Levi studied with him there. When Afes died, Hanina took the post, and Levi, left with no study partner, went to Babylonia. When Rav heard of a great limping teacher newly arrived in Neharde'a, he concluded from this that Afes had died.

people.name: Hanina bar Hama
people.about: named by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to head the yeshiva

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: older than Hanina by two and a half years

people.name: Levi
people.about: studied with Hanina outside, later went to Babylonia

people.name: Rav
people.about: drew the conclusion from the news of Levi

terms.meaning: an academy for Torah study.

ketubot-103b-24-25.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was moved from Beit She'arim to Tzippori, a higher place with better air, when he fell ill. On the day he died, the Sages fasted and prayed that he would live and threatened anyone who announced his death. His maidservant first prayed he would stay, but seeing his painful illness, she prayed he be allowed to go. She threw a jug from the roof, the sudden noise stopped the Sages' prayers, and he died. Bar Kappara told them with a hint rather than saying it. As Rabbi died, he said he had worked in the Torah with all ten fingers and had taken no benefit from the world. A heavenly voice answered that he enters in peace.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: the leader who is dying

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: sent by the Sages to check on him

terms.meaning: a heavenly voice the Talmud describes as announcing a message.
small leather boxes with Torah verses, worn on the head and arm during prayer.

ketubot-104b-7-15.note: Rav Hiyya Arikha supported his brother's widow for 25 years from his brother's estate. When she then asked for support and then for her marriage contract money, he refused. Rabba bar Sheila ruled that she could still collect, since she had likely stayed silent out of embarrassment, and gave her authorization to seize his property when he did not pay. Rava agreed with the ruling but then rejected her claim to the crops grown since. The authorization lacked a needed clause saying the land came from the dead husband's estate, and Rava held it was not a scribal slip because Rabba bar Sheila himself had not thought the clause mattered.

people.name: Rav Hiyya Arikha
people.about: called Arikha, meaning tall, because of his height

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: the judge who first ruled for the widow

people.name: Rava
people.about: rabbi who reviewed the case

terms.meaning: a document promising a wife a sum of money when the marriage ends by divorce or the husband's death.
a court document letting a creditor take a debtor's property to collect a debt.

ketubot-105b-10-11.note: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper normally brought him a basket of fruit every Shabbat eve, but one Thursday brought it early because he had a court case to bring before him. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and said he could not judge the case. He had two scholars judge it instead. Even so, he found himself thinking of arguments to help the sharecropper win, and concluded that anyone who accepts a bribe must be even more biased.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: the judge who refused the gift

terms.meaning: a farmer who works someone else's land and pays part of the crop.

ketubot-105b-12-13.note: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing of his sheep, a gift priests are due. Rabbi Yishmael asked why he came so far, and the man said he had a court case before him. Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, said he could not judge the case, and had two scholars judge it. Still, he caught himself thinking of arguments for the man and concluded that anyone who takes a bribe is bound to be biased.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
people.about: a priest

terms.meaning: the first wool cut from a flock, which the Torah says is given to a priest.
a descendant of Aaron, who is entitled to certain gifts from the people.

ketubot-105b-14-16.note: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish and said he had a case. Rav Anan declined the gift and said he could not judge the man. The man said he wanted to give it as honor to a Torah scholar, as with first fruits, so Rav Anan took it. He then sent the man to Rav Nahman with a letter saying he could not judge him. Rav Nahman assumed the man was a relative of Rav Anan, put aside an orphans' case, and honored him, so the other side lost heart and lost. Elijah the Prophet then stopped visiting Rav Anan, and when he returned he appeared in frightening forms. Rav Anan built a box to sit in until Elijah had taught him the rest of his Seder.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: the scholar who accepted the gift

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: the judge who heard the man's case

people.name: Elijah the Prophet
people.about: used to teach Rav Anan

terms.meaning: the first produce of the harvest, brought as a gift to the priests.
a Jewish book of teachings that the text says Elijah taught Rav Anan.

ketubot-106a-2-3.note: The first line finishes the previous story: Rav Anan sat in a box before Elijah until Elijah taught him his whole Seder, which is why there are a larger and a smaller Seder Eliyahu. A new story then begins: in Rav Yosef's time there was a famine, and the Sages asked him to pray for mercy. He replied that the prophet Elisha supported 2,200 Sages from his own pocket and did not pray during a famine, so why should he. The passage ends there with no further outcome.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: asked by the Sages to pray during a famine

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: in the first line, who learned Elijah's Seder

people.name: Elisha
people.about: the prophet, mentioned as a comparison

terms.meaning: a Jewish book of teachings that the text says Elijah taught Rav Anan.

ketubot-109b-3-5.note: A man set up one field as a boundary marker for a neighbor's field, which treated it as belonging to someone else. He later claimed the field was his, then died, leaving a steward managing his orphans' property. Abaye said the father had lost his right to claim it. The steward answered that the father might have meant only one edge furrow, and Abaye agreed to give that furrow. The steward then said the father might have bought the field back, saving the palm trees there, and Abaye accepted this too. Abaye said that anyone appointing a steward should choose one who defends orphans like this.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the rabbi who judged the case

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: his ruling is quoted as the basis

terms.meaning: a person appointed to manage property for orphans.

ketubot-111b-13-13.note: This is one of several tall-tale-style reports praising how fertile the Land of Israel was. Rav Yosef tells of a man in the village of Shihin whose father left him three mustard branches. One broke, and that branch alone held nine kav of mustard, and its wood roofed a booth for craftsmen. Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa adds that his father left a cabbage stalk so tall they climbed it with a ladder.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: reports the incident

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa
people.about: says his father left a cabbage stalk they climbed with a ladder

terms.meaning: a small ancient measure of volume, used for grain and similar goods.
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it.

ketubot-111b-19-20.note: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a children's teacher employed by Reish Lakish, missed three days of teaching. He explained that he had been harvesting one grapevine his father left him, which gave 300 clusters a day. On day one each cluster filled a jug with wine, on day two it took two clusters per jug, and on day three three; he declared more than half of it ownerless. Reish Lakish answered that had he not neglected the children's Torah study, each cluster would have yielded more.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Adda
people.about: a children's teacher employed by Reish Lakish

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: a rabbi, here the one who questions him

terms.meaning: the Land of Israel.

ketubot-111b-21-21.note: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under a fig tree. Honey was oozing from the figs and milk dripping from the goats, and the two were mixing together. He said that this is what the verse means by a land flowing with milk and honey.

people.name: Rami bar Yehezkel
people.about: the rabbi who saw this

ketubot-111b-22-22.note: Three rabbis describe the milk-and-honey fertility of the Land of Israel. Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai says he walked ankle-deep in honey from fig trees between Lud and Ono. Reish Lakish says he saw a region near Tzippori of sixteen by sixteen mil. Rabba bar bar Hana says the whole milk-and-honey region was 22 by 6 parasangs. These are claims about size and plenty, with no plot.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai
people.about: walked in honey from figs

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: described a region near Tzippori

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: described the whole region

terms.meaning: an ancient measure of distance, roughly two-thirds of a mile.
an ancient Persian measure of distance, equal to about eight mil.

ketubot-112a-3-4.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and saw grape clusters as big as calves. Sad that such bounty went to foreign rulers during Israel's troubled times, he said the earth might better not produce such fruit. The next year Rabbi Hiyya came and saw clusters only as big as goats, and the locals told him not to repeat what his colleague had done. The text says Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's curse had come true and the fruit had shrunk.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: saw the huge clusters and spoke the words

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: visited the next year

terms.meaning: a place in the Golan region.

ketubot-112a-11-11.note: An Amorite asked a resident of the Land of Israel how many dates he could pick from a palm tree on the Jordan bank. The man said sixty kor. The Amorite said he had harmed the land, since they used to pick 120 kor from that tree. The man replied he was speaking of only one side of the tree and had not yet picked the other. It is a boasting exchange about the land's fertility.

terms.meaning: a member of one of the peoples who lived in Canaan before Israel.
a large ancient measure of volume, about 30 se'ah.

ketubot-112a-16-16.note: Rabbi Zeira came to enter the Land of Israel but found no ferry over the Jordan, so he crossed holding a rope strung across the river. A Sadducee mocked him as hasty, like those who said we will do before we will hear at Sinai. Rabbi Zeira answered that Moses and Aaron did not merit entering the land, so he hurried across before anything could stop him.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: crossed the Jordan on a rope

terms.meaning: a member of a Jewish group of the time that rejected the oral tradition the rabbis taught.

terms.term: we will do before we will hear
terms.meaning: the words of Israel at Sinai (Exodus 24:7), taken to mean they agreed to follow the Torah before hearing it.
